catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q1.explanation: B - advancedWhen we talk of an advanced age, we mean that somebody is older than anybody else in this situation. It is quite unusual to pick up any sports (even racing) at the age of 37. We could use ‘ancient’ to refer to somebody who is truly old – well over 70, for instance. The word ‘mature’ is more about having a well-developed emotional side, not talking so much about the age itself.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q2.explanation: A - earnedTo earn (a) reputation is a common collocation. To deserve a reputation would be more appropriate if we were talking about something negative.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q3.explanation: B - handicap‘Handicap’ implies a disadvantage she had to overcome, fitting the context of her late start and gender. There is a common stereotype that women can be worse drivers than men, more so in the competitive setting like a race. ‘Obstacle’ shouldn’t be chosen because of the indefinite ‘a’ article.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q4.explanation: C - concentrationBecause of her piloting background, her ability to concentrate came in handy in races. ‘Fixation’ is something you are so focused on and obsessed with that it becomes a problem. ‘Attention’ and ‘commitment’ do not convey the necessary meaning here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q5.explanation: C - knownTo be best known is another common collocation you should know at this level. ‘Best remembered’ is not nearly as common.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q6.explanation: A - performingThe idea here is that she was performing the role of the race car driver.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q7.explanation: C - forTo speak for itself means to be evident enough to be noticed. The meaning here is that she wanted to prove her worth as a driver through actions rather than words.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-1-q8.explanation: D - stageA stage of your life is a big part of it, especially one that is associated with a particular period (in this case, being a professional driver). ‘Half’ could probably be used in the context of ‘either half of your life’, where ‘either’ shows one of the two options (the first half and the second half). ‘Phase’ means one of the several parts in something and indicates some kind of planning, e.g. ‘the first phase of the operation’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q9.explanation: asWe use ‘as much as’ to mention a certain number. Note that the author uses ‘much’ and not ‘many’ because we refer to the weight itself, not the number.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q10.explanation: howTo baffle means to confuse, to be a source of questions. The scientists couldn’t understand why (or how) the rocks moved on their own.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q11.explanation: rangingA number of possible reasons for rocks moving are mentioned in the text. Another thing to note is that we could do without any word in the gap. However, keep in mind that you should never be leaving empty gaps in CAE Use of English Part 2, as an empty gap is never going to be the right answer.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q12.explanation: thatThe structure goes ‘It wasn’t until … that’ and it is a set one, meaning you shouldn’t be changing it. The temptation to use ‘when’ is understandable, but it doesn’t make the set structure and therefore shouldn’t be chosen.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q13.explanation: if/whenThis is a zero conditional sentence – one that speaks about things that are always true. ‘If’ or ‘when’ to introduce the condition and sentence in the Present Simple to show the result.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q14.explanation: onWe use ‘on’ to talk about particular days, be it days of the week or dates.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q15.explanation: it‘All it takes’ shows how little is required to achieve something.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-2-q16.explanation: behindThe trails (traces, paths) that are left behind the moving rocks.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q17.explanation: commercialAdjective that keeps the double ‘m’ in the root.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q18.explanation: abilityEven though ‘shoppers’ is in the plural, ‘ability’ doesn’t have to be.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q19.explanation: unattainableIf something is unattainable, it means that it is impossible to get. In this case, consumers of foods made by large companies will never have the level of trust and familiarity they have with the small local sellers.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q20.explanation: awarenessGrowing knowledge and realisation of environmental impact is what they are talking about here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q21.explanation: sustainableSomething that can be sustained (supported) over longer periods of time.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q22.explanation: exceedingDon’t be fooled into answering ‘excellent’, as the key verb would have to be ‘excel’ then.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q23.explanation: immenselyAn adverb that is very easy to misspell.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-3-q24.explanation: producersThe plural form is here because the word ‘producer’ is countable, and if used in the singular would need an article, either ‘a local producer’ or ‘the local producer’, both fitting just fine.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q25.explanation: sooner had we landedThe idea here is that one thing took place immediately after the other. In this case we use inversion, putting the auxiliary verb ‘had’ before the subject (I).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q26.answer: apologised for not having called/not calling
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q26.explanation: apologised for not having called/apologised for not callingWe are free to use either the more complex Present Gerund (‘not having called’) or the simple gerund form. The first one is better in showing that the call (or the absence of the call) happened before the apology took place.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q27.explanation: might not have got/receivedA thing to note here is that the tense changed from Past Simple in the original sentence to Past Perfect in the answer.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q28.explanation: only I had appliedWe use structures like ‘if only’ to show regret. In other words, the speaker is sorry that he didn’t do something in the past.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q29.explanation: has been two years sinceAs the answer has to have ‘since’ in it, it also forces us to use a Perfect tense. Present Perfect fits here just fine.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-4-q30.explanation: led to the cancellationPlease note that the definite article is needed as a part of the ‘of’ structure.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-5-q31.explanation: BLooking at the process of making things out of clay charmed the author and made him try it himself. Answer A is incorrect – no real technical or in-depth information is given. Author makes no criticism of any kind in the first paragraph. Paragraph Two mentions how hard the process actually is, but again, without any complaint towards online tutorials. Finally, there is no comparison of different learning methods.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-5-q32.explanation: BA couple of words lead us here to choose answer B. ‘Strenuous’ means requiring physical effort. ‘My arms ached’ refers to the amount of effort required for wedging. Even though operating the wheel is mentioned (‘it was just a wamp-up for the main event), there is no direct comparison in difficulty. And while it was difficult, the author doesn’t say that they didn’t enjoy the process.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-5-q33.explanation: DThe word ‘humbled’ means that the author suddenly was much less sure about their own skills and felt that people who can do that well deserve respect. The instructor is only mentioned in the context of them being quite good at centring, no criticism expressed. Answer B doesn’t work, as the author doesn’t say anything about hoping to get better.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-5-q34.explanation: CThis part of Paragraph 4 sets the positive tone of the correct answer: ‘The noise and demands of the outside world faded away…’. All other options have a clear negative meaning, which is absent in the paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-5-q35.explanation: AThe crucial part is in Paragraph 5: ‘…almost looking forward to more disappointment…’. The sudden breakthrough came as an unexpected, but pleasant surprise. Answer B mentions a minor detail – how much failed attempts it took to finally achieve something. The instructor’s input once again fails to get mentioned.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-5-q36.explanation: BAnswer C shouldn’t be chosen because they do not add value on their own. Instead, they become the living proof of their man-made nature. Answer D is not ideal either – it is indeed true that machines can avoid them, but it is not directly stated in the text, nor is it the focal point of the paragraph. Nothing is mentioned about room for improvement; the author accepts the fact that his art has flaws, nothing else.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-6-q37.explanation: CBoth A and C comment on a lack of deep emotional connection. A is saying the characters are ‘at a certain emotional arm’s length, and that they work as vessels (devices) rather than real characters. C concurs, mentioning that the author ‘neglects to forge a deep emotional connection’, and that it is difficult to relate to the character’s choices.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-6-q38.explanation: CReviewer C mentions that the themes of the books ‘feel strikingly relevant to our modern era of misinformation’. Reviewer D raises a similar point, saying that ‘the more attentive readers are likely to see references to the political landscape of today’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-6-q39.explanation: DReviewers A, B, and C all, to varying degrees, find the protagonist somewhat emotionally distant or passive. Reviewer D explicitly disagrees, finding the character’s journey ‘entirely compelling and emotionally resonant’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-6-q40.explanation: DReviewer A finds the narrative to be ‘deliberately slow’ and potentially trying readers’ patience, while Reviewer D argues the deliberate pace ‘serves to build an almost unbearable psychological tension,’ viewing it as a strength.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-7-q41.explanation: CIt follows the introduction of the term “slow productivity” by explaining the basics, letting the reader know what it is. This is later contrasted with “performative busyness” in the next sentence.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-7-q42.explanation: GParagraph G logically follows the mentioned “hustle culture” by explaining the negative consequences of its pressure, leading into the next paragraph about tools that worsen the problem.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-7-q43.explanation: BIt provides a concrete, practical example of the principle mentioned in the previous sentence: “focusing on one significant project at a time.” The example of the writer illustrates this perfectly.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-7-q44.explanation: AThis paragraph explains why exactly the “protected downtime” mentioned in the previous sentence is so important, citing the neurological and creative benefits of rest and how it is an investment rather than wasted time.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-7-q45.explanation: FParagraph F addresses the “challenges” and “fear” mentioned in the previous paragraph, specifying where this pressure is intense (finance and law) and introducing the counter-argument about burnout.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-7-q46.explanation: DThe theme of the previous paragraph about workplace culture gets a continuation, showing a positive solution and how „forward-thinking companies” are implementing the article’s ideas, leading to the concluding paragraph about sustainability.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q47.explanation: ABen mentions that you have to invest heavily into this hobby and gives a list of things that one has to buy before they can enjoy it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q48.explanation: CDavid talks about the joy of exploration, finding new things in the neighbourhood they wouldn’t have if it weren’t for their bike.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q49.explanation: DLast sentence of Sarah’s paragraph has her sharing how she benefitted from cycling in a non-fitness way.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q50.explanation: BThe process of riding and focusing on the road allows them to ‘decompress’ – that is, to leave their worries behind, to forget about things that trouble them.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q51.explanation: DUnderstanding all the dangers of urban cycling and reacting to them is ‘a complex skill set that one slowly builds over time’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q52.explanation: AThe aggressive drivers are what Ben is unhappy about. Note that even though Sarah (D) mentions similar aspect, she doesn’t seem to be angry at them.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q53.explanation: ABeating the traffic isn’t easy, but cycling seems to work for Ben.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q54.explanation: AWhile Ben had to invest a lot of money initially, cycling has allowed him to save a lot of money: ‘I’ve recouped that cost many times over’

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q55.explanation: CLast part of Sarah’s paragraph gives reasons why cycling might not appeal to some people because of its dangerous nature.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test22-part-8-q56.explanation: CThe beginning of the paragraph mentions David feeling liberation – something he hadn’t had since he was a child.
